messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame Mensah is a 47-year-old park ranger who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle it on his own. He grew up in West Africa and, as a civilian during a period of armed conflict, survived an attack in a rural area where brush had been set alight and people fled through fields and trees. In the first session he spoke haltingly about the worst part: being ordered at gunpoint to help men he feared, doing things he now experiences as a betrayal of the person he believed himself to be, and then living when others around him did not. What remains most vivid to him is the orange movement of flames along dry ground, the smell of smoke in open air, and the feeling that danger could be hidden anywhere in a landscape that looked peaceful until it suddenly was not.

For years he kept working outdoors, eventually becoming a park ranger in the United States, but the setting that once felt meaningful now catches him off guard. A small campfire at a legal fire ring, sunlight flashing like flame through dry grass, or even being corrected by a supervisor on trail procedure can jolt him into the same constricted state. When visitors burn brush illegally or he sees flames at the edge of woodland, he feels his chest tighten before he has fully registered what he is looking at. On patrol in the woods, especially in isolated stretches that resemble the rural terrain where the attack happened, he becomes unable to relax despite knowing, intellectually, that he is in a protected park and not a war zone. If a coworker is late answering the radio, or a maintenance crew takes longer than expected to check in, he quickly assumes something bad has happened.

Those moments do not stop with fear. Being corrected by someone in authority can carry an immediate sting of shame, as if criticism proves what he already suspects about himself: that he failed morally and survived at others’ expense. Fire in the landscape and time alone in nature also pull him toward memories of the people who died and toward the part of the event he cannot forgive in himself. He has come to believe he is set apart from other people, not simply because they do not know what happened, but because if they did, they would see him as contaminated by what he did to stay alive. In turn, these beliefs make the world feel less safe. At night he lies awake replaying who was lost and what he did, and the guilt keeps his body keyed up. Even minor delays begin to feel ominous, as though disaster is always just out of sight.

Over time Kwame has organized his life around getting through these reactions. He has cut off most contact with friends and family, ignoring calls rather than trying to explain himself. He drinks in the evenings to blunt the agitation enough to get a few hours of sleep. Although his work brings him into regular contact with law enforcement in the park, he changes his route when he sees police uniforms, avoids joint assignments that involve armed officers, and keeps his distance from anything that reminds him of weapons. When criticism, flames, or certain wooded areas set him off, withdrawing and drinking feel like the quickest ways to get out of his own skin.

But these habits have narrowed his life and deepened what he believes about himself. The more completely he isolates, the more convinced he becomes that he does not belong with other people. Avoiding officers and anything linked to weapons leaves those sights feeling even more charged when he cannot escape them. Drinking leaves him groggy and ashamed in the morning, and after poor sleep he is even more watchful on the job, scanning the tree line and reacting strongly if someone is delayed or if smoke appears in the distance. In that state, being in the park itself becomes more loaded; ordinary natural settings increasingly feel like places where something terrible is about to happen. He notices criticism more sharply too, bracing for it and hearing correction as accusation.

What finally brought him in was an incident at work when a controlled burn was being discussed and a supervisor tersely corrected him in front of others. Kwame left his shift early, drank heavily that night, and did not answer his phone for two days. He said he is frightened that he is becoming impossible to work with and that if this continues he will lose the one part of his life that still gives him structure. At the same time, he is hoping—carefully, almost reluctantly—that treatment might help him sleep, stop living as if every delay means catastrophe, and face the woods he works in without feeling that the past is waiting there for him.
